{"id": "9:76/q11", "question": "What occasion or sequence of events is reported for this verse?", "turns_on": "Reports differ over a multiplying flock, inherited wealth, an unnamed Anṣārī, two assembly participants, or a general group; al-Suyuti flags a weak report and Kur'an Yolu disputes common historical attributions.", "positions": [{"id": "9:76/q11/p1", "position": "Tha'laba sought wealth, gained a multiplying flock after the Prophet's prayer, neglected worship, refused zakat, and his later offer was rejected.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, al-Bursawi, Elmalılı, Ibn Ashur and Study Quran relay stages of the account. The Prophet warned that thankable little wealth is better than unmanageable plenty (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Elmalılı); Tha'laba pledged every person's due, moved out of Medina as sheep multiplied and abandoned congregation then Friday prayer (al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Kathir, Elmalılı). Collectors brought a written order after zakat was imposed (Ibn Atiyya); he called zakat a tax like jizya and delayed (Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tha'labi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, Elmalılı). A Sulami man freely gave choice camels, and the Prophet blessed him (Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir). The Prophet lamented Tha'laba, in some versions before hearing the collectors (al-Baghawi, al-Bursawi, Elmalılı). A relative or Umar warned Tha'laba of revelation (al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bursawi). The Prophet said God forbade accepting the later offer; Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman also refused it, and Tha'laba died under Uthman (al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, al-Bursawi, Elmalılı, Ibn Ashur). Al-Bursawi attributes his distress to public shame rather than repentance and cites al-Haddadi for Uthman's refusal. Al-Suyuti labels Abu Umama's report weak and also gives an Ibn Abbas version. Ibn Kathir links 9:103 to the case. Kur'an Yolu objects that common occasion reports conflict with historical evidence."}, {"id": "9:76/q11/p2", "position": "Tha'laba inherited wealth from a cousin after promising charity, kin care and every due, but failed to keep that promise.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi attributes the inheritance account to Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada; al-Hasan in al-Durr also says the Anṣārī inherited his cousin's wealth and hypocrisy followed the broken promise."}, {"id": "9:76/q11/p3", "position": "An unnamed Anṣārī at an assembly promised to distribute rightful dues if enriched but acted otherwise.", "reasons": "Qatada in al-Tabari gives the assembly and vow without naming the man."}, {"id": "9:76/q11/p4", "position": "Two men left an assembly after vowing charity if enriched, but withheld it when wealth came.", "reasons": "Mujahid in al-Tabari gives two unnamed men; al-Hasan and Mujahid in al-Baghawi identify the pair as Tha'laba and Mu'attib and call their vow public."}, {"id": "9:76/q11/p5", "position": "A group of hypocrites promised charity and righteousness if enriched but broke the promise.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri says they remained trapped in hypocrisy; Ibn Kathir and al-Tabatabai describe a group of hypocrites. Ibn Zayd compares their unrepentant persistence until meeting God to Iblis."}]}
{"id": "9:76/q12", "question": "Was their pledge spoken aloud?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding covenant was a public vow or an unspoken intention; Sa'id invokes 9:78 for the latter.", "positions": [{"id": "9:76/q12/p1", "position": "The pledge was publicly spoken.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas in al-Tabari says Tha'laba pledged publicly; Qatada places the vow at an assembly, and al-Hasan and Mujahid describe the two men's public vow."}, {"id": "9:76/q12/p2", "position": "It was an inward intention, never voiced.", "reasons": "Some authorities and Sa'id ibn Thabit say this. Sa'id appeals to 9:78 on God's knowledge of secrets and private conversations. Mu'tamir recounts an analogous unspoken sea-storm vow; his father Sulayman told him to voice or fulfill it."}]}
{"id": "9:76/q13", "question": "What does this passage establish about signs of hypocrisy?", "turns_on": "Whether the familiar three-trait hadith gives a universal diagnostic or describes particular hypocrites; Ata's example of Joseph's brothers and the reported Prophetic clarification support restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "9:76/q13/p1", "position": "Lying, breaking promises and betraying trusts or covenants are three signs of hypocrisy.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari cites Companions, Successors and Prophetic reports; Abdullah, Abdullah ibn Amr, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar and Muhammad ibn Ka'b recite this passage, with Muhammad ibn Ka'b also invoking 33:72 and 63:1. Prophetic versions in al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi and al-Durr say the traits mark a hypocrite even if he prays, fasts and claims Islam. Abdullah ibn Amr or his father honored a marriage promise on his deathbed for fear of one-third hypocrisy; al-Hasan's question about an insolvent debtor shows his concern about a blanket application. In an account in al-Tha'labi, Muqatil ibn Hayyan feared for himself and all people, left his judgeship, asked scholars in Bukhara, Merv and Nishapur, was directed by Shahr to Sa'id in Ray, and Sa'id sent him to Hasan. Al-Hasan initially answers that the hadith is as transmitted. Al-Tabari connects broken promises and lying in 9:75-77 to hypocrisy."}, {"id": "9:76/q13/p2", "position": "Four marks constitute complete hypocrisy: lying, breaking promises, betraying covenants and indecency in dispute.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi transmits an Ibn Umar report through Masruq that any one remains a mark until abandoned."}, {"id": "9:76/q13/p3", "position": "The hadith's three traits refer specifically to the hypocrites who lied to the Prophet, betrayed his trust and broke their campaign pledge.", "reasons": "Ata cites Joseph's brothers, who committed the three acts without being hypocrites, against a universal reading. Jabir says the intended men lied to the Prophet, disclosed his confidential report of Abu Sufyan's location and failed to campaign, connecting 8:27 with 9:75-77. Al-Hasan accepts Ata's account. Al-Tha'labi warns that the hadith's apparent wording can mislead; in his account Hasan says Shahr heard half the report, Fatima conveyed the Companions' alarm, and the Prophet publicly clarified the restriction. The Prophet relates their false faith claim to 63:1, their prayer and religious trust to 4:142 and 107:4-5, and their broken promise to Tha'laba's charity pledge. Their clarification relieved the Companions, who gave generously."}]}
{"id": "9:76/q14", "question": "What moral consequence or guidance do the sources draw from their conduct?", "turns_on": "The notes draw related consequences of punishment, loss of trustworthy conduct, and abiding hypocrisy, without opposing one another.", "positions": [{"id": "9:76/q14/p1", "position": "Turning away from repentance and obedience incurs punishment, so the warning urges obedience and deters sin.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi draws this warning from their turn away."}, {"id": "9:76/q14/p2", "position": "Self-interested promises followed by stinginess show faith failing to govern conduct and destroy responsibility and trust.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu contrasts this with Prophetic reports that deeds depend on intentions and that one may be rewarded for intending good even if unable to do it; its point concerns people who can act but choose not to."}, {"id": "9:76/q14/p3", "position": "The unrepentant withholding leaves hypocrisy in their hearts until they meet God.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says there was no repentance, forgiveness or pardon, comparing Iblis; al-Qushayri says the broken covenant trapped them in hypocrisy; al-Hasan in al-Durr says the broken promise brought hypocrisy until death."}]}
{"id": "9:76/q15", "question": "What response to withheld zakat is reported?", "turns_on": "These are distinct reported responses to withheld zakat; the notes do not claim they address the same case.", "positions": [{"id": "9:76/q15/p1", "position": "The Prophet refused Tha'laba's belated offering by God's order, and the first three caliphs likewise refused it.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, al-Bursawi, Elmalılı and Ibn Ashur transmit the refusal; the Prophet also called it a consequence of his prior disobedience. Reports differ in detail over which caliphs are individually named, while the fuller accounts include Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman."}, {"id": "9:76/q15/p2", "position": "Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told an official to leave a zakat withholder to the contempt his act would incur.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this response to an official's notice of nonpayment."}]}
{"id": "9:76/q16", "question": "How does this verse connect with its surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "The sources draw distinct links to the adjacent covenant and requital, the sura's wider portrait, 9:103, and illustrative commands and promises.", "positions": [{"id": "9:76/q16/p1", "position": "The passage escalates from ingratitude without a pledge to the graver ingratitude of betraying an explicit covenant.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says the next verse's grave requital, 9:77, underscores the seriousness of that betrayal. Ibn Ashur says the charity pledge explains the earlier covenant in 9:75."}, {"id": "9:76/q16/p2", "position": "The verse belongs to a broader portrayal of hypocrites, including criticism of believers' donations.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai juxtaposes the enriched pledge-breakers with hypocrites who criticized both affluent and poor donors, all condemned as hypocrites beyond forgiveness. Al-Jishumi says they could fault nothing except that God enriched them from His bounty. Abu Qilaba likens sectarian followers of desire to hypocrites, citing 9:58 and 9:61 alongside this passage. Study Quran notes the sura's other general descriptions of hypocr

ites."}, {"id": "9:76/q16/p3", "position": "The account associates the charity command in 9:103 with Tha'laba's case.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports the connection, and al-Suyuti's weak Abu Umama account and Ibn Abbas version also mention 9:103."}, {"id": "9:76/q16/p4", "position": "The passage exemplifies the warning against neglected divine commands and broken pledges.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari transmits the Prophet's account of Israelites asking Moses for three manageable commands instead of the Torah, then neglecting even those. Another Prophetic promise offers Paradise to those who avoid lying, promise-breaking and betrayal and guard eyes, hands and private parts from betrayal, theft and adultery."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q01", "question": "Whom does the opening 'they' address?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun continues the account of the covenant makers alone or broadens the warning to all hypocrites.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q01/p1", "position": "The hypocrites generally, including those who made and broke the covenant.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the warning applies to all hypocrites. Abū Ḥayyān calls this the apparent scope and explicitly includes the covenant breakers. Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī allow the hypocrites as the implied subject."}, {"id": "9:78/q01/p2", "position": "The group who made the preceding covenant.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this restriction from the interpreter who regards the pact as an inward intention. Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī allow covenant makers as the subject; Bursevī treats their knowledge as acknowledged."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q02", "question": "What is the force of 'Did they not know?'", "turns_on": "Whether the interrogative chiefly censures the culprits, confirms what they know, or alerts listeners.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q02/p1", "position": "It rebukes and warns the hypocrites for acting despite God's knowledge.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī says they ought to know what God knows; Abū Ḥayyān calls it censure. Rāzī says they conspire despite knowing God sees and punishes hidden acts like public ones. Qurṭubī makes requital the point; Ālūsī says it threatens grave acts and the explicit divine name magnifies awe and reckoning. Elmalılı and Ṭabāṭabāʾī call it reproach. Qushayrī compares warnings by God's knowledge here with warnings by His acts elsewhere."}, {"id": "9:78/q02/p2", "position": "It confirms that the covenant makers already knew of God's knowledge, prompting acknowledgment of requital.", "reasons": "Bursevī identifies a confirmatory question to the covenant makers. Ālūsī allows a prompt to acknowledge that God will punish and requite them."}, {"id": "9:78/q02/p3", "position": "It alerts listeners to an important matter.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites this verse alongside 9:63 as a parallel interrogative serving that purpose."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q03", "question": "How is 'know' read, and whom does the alternate reading address?", "turns_on": "The yāʾ or tāʾ reading and whether a second-person address turns to believers or remains directed at the prior group.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q03/p1", "position": "The majority read yaʿlamū, in the third person, concerning the hypocrites or covenant makers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the majority reading; al-Samīn calls it that of most readers. Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī give the two possible third-person subjects."}, {"id": "9:78/q03/p2", "position": "Taʿlamū reads with second-person tāʾ and addresses believers, assuring or admonishing them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya names Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and al-Ḥasan; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and Biqāʿī also name ʿAlī. Abū Ḥayyān says God gradually exposes the hypocrites to believers; Biqāʿī says this knowledge benefits those prepared for faith. Bayḍāwī mentions the shift; Ālūsī reports ʿAlī's reading."}, {"id": "9:78/q03/p3", "position": "The second-person reading addresses the first group by a shift in person.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this alternative but calls it strained because the continuation speaks of God knowing 'their' secrets and private conversation."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q04", "question": "How does this verse bear on the preceding covenant?", "turns_on": "What can be inferred from this verse's mention of secrets and from a restricted use of language in the preceding context.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q04/p1", "position": "Mention of secrets supports taking the preceding vow as including an unspoken intention.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya links the opening to the interpretation that the pact was made inwardly. Rāzī reports proponents who include both a spoken promise and a silent intention in a vow and cite this verse's secrets and private counsel."}, {"id": "9:78/q04/p2", "position": "A restriction proved for one usage does not restrict every usage of the earlier expression 'meeting'.", "reasons": "Rāzī rejects extending evidence that excludes vision in a particular use of meeting to all other uses; this is his objection to that broader inference in the surrounding discussion."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q05", "question": "What is meant by 'their secret'?", "turns_on": "Whether 'secret' denotes inward states, a specific concealed belief or intention, the Aqaba plot, or quiet speech.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q05/p1", "position": "What they conceal inwardly, in their hearts or breasts.", "reasons": "Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Rāzī, Ṭabrisī, Biqāʿī, and Elmalılı describe inward concealment. Qushayrī and Sulamī say only God, the Knower of secrets, sees it; Sulamī contrasts private talk accessible to recording angels. Ibn Kathīr includes inner motives even behind professed charity. Study Quran says sirr can name either the secret itself or a thing's hidden or mysterious aspect."}, {"id": "9:78/q05/p2", "position": "Their concealed disbelief or hypocrisy, despite professing faith.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and al-Ḥasan with Qatāda in Jishumī contrast hidden denial of God, His Messenger, or Muhammad with public profession to believers. Bayḍāwī offers inward hypocrisy; Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī and another view; Nasafī and Ālūsī apply it to hypocrites."}, {"id": "9:78/q05/p3", "position": "Their concealed intent to break their covenant.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī offers it as an alternative to inward hypocrisy. Nasafī joins it with hypocrisy. Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī; Bursevī and Ālūsī explain it for the covenant makers."}, {"id": "9:78/q05/p4", "position": "The plot of the Aqaba people to kill the Prophet.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies the secret and private conversation with the plot they agreed upon."}, {"id": "9:78/q05/p5", "position": "What some say quietly to one another, contrasted with their more open discussion together.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this further explanation and says it is close to the other interpretations."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q06", "question": "What does 'their private conversation' mean or contain?", "turns_on": "Whether najwā is defined broadly as confidential speech or identified with a particular hostile discussion, plot, inward discourse, or relatively open group talk.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q06/p1", "position": "Confidential speech among themselves.", "reasons": "Qushayrī, Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Biqāʿī, and Elmalılı describe speech or discussion among confidants. Ṭabrisī lists nājā, tanājā, intajā, and plural anjiya, deriving the root from remoteness or a raised place safe from flood; Rāzī likewise derives it from an isolated elevation where speakers exclude others and cites 19:52, 12:80, 58:9, 58:12. Bursevī gives najāhu/nājāhu and the sense of confidential speech; Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Study Quran define it similarly. Sulamī says recording angels can see it, unlike their secret. Ibn Kathīr includes private talk and inner motives."}, {"id": "9:78/q06/p2", "position": "Their speech attacks Islam, the Prophet, believers, or the religion.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says they speak improperly of Islam and adherents; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds plotting against the Prophet, community, and law. Bayḍāwī says attacks among themselves. Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī and another view specifying denigration of the Prophet and believers. Nasafī and Ālūsī mention religious attacks or mutual slander. Study Quran cites related private-talk passages: 4:114, 17:47, 20:62, 21:3, 43:80, 58:7-8, 58:10, 58:12-13."}, {"id": "9:78/q06/p3", "position": "They call zakāt a poll tax and discuss withholding alms.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī mentions calling zakāt jizya; Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān's report from al-Zamakhsharī add a plan to withhold it. Bursevī includes other speech devoid of good, secret or public; Ālūsī applies this account to covenant makers."}, {"id": "9:78/q06/p4", "position": "The agreed Aqaba plot to kill the Prophet.", "reasons": "Muqātil applies both their secret and private conversation to this plot."}, {"id": "9:78/q06/p5", "position": "Their inner thoughts as surveyed by their own souls.", "reasons": "Qushayrī says najwā may extend from confidential speech to this inward discourse."}, {"id": "9:78/q06/p6", "position": "What they discuss openly together, contrasted with quiet speech called their secret.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the distinction and regards the explanations as close in meaning."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q07", "question": "Why is 'secret' mentioned before 'private conversation'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q07/p1", "position": "Knowing the deeper secret inspires greater awe, so mentioning it first hastens awe or reassurance.", "reasons": "Ālūsī says secret knowledge is more awe-inspiring in ordinary perception; its effect can be fear or reassurance depending on the reading."}]}

n Jishumī says they already acknowledge the God who knows both. Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda specify concealed rejection and professed faith; Abū ʿAlī and Abū Muslim state the scope generally. Another Jishumī explanation says their deceptions cannot fool such a knower. Jishumī defines iʿlān as manifestation perceptible to others, opposite isrār; Abū Muslim grounds their duty to know in God's established signs and proofs. Ṭabarī applies it to outward faith and inward disbelief and says they should cease deceiving God's allies. Ibn Kathīr says even motives behind charity are known, along with hidden and manifest things. Biqāʿī says apparent enrichment might fool an ignorant observer, while God's judgment of hearts proves His knowledge exceeds each person's self-knowledge."}, {"id": "9:78/q08/p2", "position": "God knows even deeds not yet done but destined to be done.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, says this is more hidden than a secret."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q09", "question": "What is meant by 'the unseen things'?", "turns_on": "Whether the account explicitly includes nonexistent knowables as well as real things beyond current perception.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q09/p1", "position": "Things beyond creatures' sight, hearing, senses, or present perception, including concealed hearts.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī lists created beings' hearing, sight, senses, and hearts. Rāzī says creatures cannot perceive the unseen. Study Quran calls it real things absent from present sense perception or belonging to another time or state, and cites 2:3."}, {"id": "9:78/q09/p2", "position": "Every thing absent from bodily or human perception, whether existent or nonexistent, insofar as it can be known.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī gives this broad account of the plural and says the form is intensive."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q10", "question": "How is 'al-ghuyūb' read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q10/p1", "position": "Al-ghiyūb with kasra and al-ghuyūb with ḍamma are canonical plurals of ghayb with the same meaning.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER says the kasra may reflect dialect and that the vocalizations make no semantic difference."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q11", "question": "What does calling God 'ʿAllām of the unseen things' assert?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q11/p1", "position": "God knows every unseen thing, so no secret can be hidden from Him.", "reasons": "Baghawī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Biqāʿī, and Ālūsī state universal knowledge; Bayḍāwī explicitly concludes none of this is hidden. Rāzī argues God's essence entails knowledge of everything including inner thoughts and compares the title with Jesus' words in 5:116. Ṭabrisī says the plural and form intensify the claim. Ibn Kathīr includes all hidden and manifest, unseen and witnessed things. Ṭabarī specifies things beyond creatures' senses and concealed in hearts."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q12", "question": "What do the verb and the form 'ʿAllām' contribute to the wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q12/p1", "position": "The verb depicts continually renewed knowledge of successive secrets; the intensive noun conveys abiding, abundant knowledge of countless unseen things.", "reasons": "Ālūsī explicitly contrasts the verbal and nominal forms and says their combination gives the sentence force and eloquence. Rāzī says ʿallām intensifies ʿālim; Ṭabrisī likewise calls the form intensive."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q13", "question": "Can God be called 'ʿallāma'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q13/p1", "position": "No; ʿallāma suggests knowledge gained through effort, which is impossible for God.", "reasons": "Rāzī distinguishes this form from the divine title ʿallām."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q14", "question": "What practical warning follows from God's knowledge here?", "turns_on": "Whether the stated consequence is a call to reform under threat or proof established by God's prior generosity.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q14/p1", "position": "The hypocrites should fear punishment, stop their deception, repent, and fulfill their covenant.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī urges fear of punishment, desistance, and repentance. Rāzī says hidden conspiracy is seen and punished like public action. Qurṭubī says God will requite them; Ālūsī similarly connects knowing to punishment. Biqāʿī says God knows their dealings and outcome, cannot be deceived, and they should fulfill their covenant. Bursevī cites a Persian couplet warning against contemplating disobedience while knowing God sees."}, {"id": "9:78/q14/p2", "position": "God's provision to people whose betrayal He knew establishes the proof against them.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī connects God's prior knowledge, His giving, and their responsibility."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q15", "question": "What does disclosure of their secrets show in the passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q15/p1", "position": "It exposes hypocrites who recognized the truth but obstinately abandoned it, and is a sign of the Prophet's miracle.", "reasons": "Jishumī grounds the warning in their obstinate rejection and treats the disclosure itself as miraculous."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q16", "question": "What report illustrates the traits of hypocrisy and private fidelity?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q16/p1", "position": "A hypocrite lies, breaks promises, and betrays trusts; believers guard the religious trust even privately.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī transmits the Prophet's three signs and calls the report sound. Qurṭubī reports Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet explained and reassured them, connecting lying, broken promises, and trust to 63:1, 9:75, and 33:72."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q17", "question": "How broadly do the reported hypocrisy traits apply?", "turns_on": "Whether the traits by themselves confer the designation, require predominance, or must be distinguished from disbelief and from hypocrisy of belief.", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q17/p1", "position": "The traits apply broadly; one characterized by them remains a hypocrite until the Resurrection.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī says many Successors and imams adopted a broad reading; he reports this as the apparent view of al-Bukhārī and other scholars."}, {"id": "9:78/q17/p2", "position": "The traits designate a hypocrite only when they predominate in the person's character.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports this from a group."}, {"id": "9:78/q17/p3", "position": "Such sins alone do not make a person an unbeliever or necessarily a hypocrite; belief and conduct must be distinguished.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī says even predominant sins do not amount to unbelief unless belief is affected. Qurṭubī's scholars cite Joseph's brothers breaking a pledge, lying, and betraying Joseph without being hypocrites; ʿAṭāʾ says they were prophets. Al-Ḥasan distinguishes hypocrisy of lying in the Prophet's time from hypocrisy of conduct continuing to the Resurrection. Al-Bukhārī reports Ḥudhayfa that hypocrisy was in the Prophet's time, whereas later it is unbelief after faith."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q18", "question": "How does the surrounding passage portray conduct and hypocrisy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q18/p1", "position": "It shows people whose professed faith does not govern conduct, exposing hypocrisy in its context and timing.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu draws this lesson from the passage."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q19", "question": "What is the 'day they meet God' in the neighboring passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q19/p1", "position": "The Day of Resurrection.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu explains the earlier phrase this way."}]}
{"id": "9:78/q20", "question": "How do virtuous people's private dealings contrast with the hypocrites'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:78/q20/p1", "position": "They accept God's provision, worship, remember Him unseen, and make their private discourse worship rather than mockery.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this contrast from Aj."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q01", "question": "What occasion prompted the command to take charity?", "turns_on": "Whether the command addresses the repentant stay-behinds, Abū Lubāba alone, or a different alms episode.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q01/p1", "position": "Repentant men who stayed behind offered their wealth; the Prophet awaited revelation, then accepted charity.", "reasons": "Muqātil says three men brought the wealth that held them back. Elmalılı allows that the Prophet's initial refusal concerned earlier refusal of alms from people such as Ḥāṭib ibn Saʿlaba."}, {"id": "9:103/q01/p2", "position": "The command arose from Abū Lubāba's repentance over warning Banū Qurayẓa by pointing to his throat.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and al-Bāqir identify him alone; reports describe his binding himself to a pillar and fasting until forgiven. {"id": "9:103/q03", "question": "May officials compel payment, and does payment to an unjust collector discharge it?", "turns_on": "Whether collection power includes force, and whether intention suffices under unjust collection.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q03/p1", "position": "The imam can forcibly collect from a refuser.", "reasons": "Al-Ikhtiyār cites the verse for collection and placement where due; Abū Bakr fought withholders, swearing even an ʿiqāl or ʿanāq formerly paid must be given."}, {"id": "9:103/q03/p2", "position": "Officials should not seize zakat by force; the owner must pay personally.", "reasons": "Al-Ashbāh reports this as the relied-upon school position. {"id": "9:103/q04", "question": "What does 'take' mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q04/p1", "position": "It means accept the offered charity.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī lists covenant, judgment, alms and pardon as senses of acceptance, while a cited passage denies acceptance of ransom. {"id": "9:103/q05", "question": "How much of their wealth was taken or required?", "turns_on": "Whether 'from' and the occasion establish a third, or external zakat specifications govern the portion.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q05/p1", "position": "The Prophet took one third and left two thirds.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and later reporters infer this from 'from their wealth,' not all wealth. {"id": "9:103/q06", "question": "How does 'from their wealth' work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Its attachment to the verb or to the following indefinite charity.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q06/p1", "position": "Min is partitive and the phrase attaches to 'take'.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this strongest; al-Ṭabrisī says all wealth need not be given. {"id": "9:103/q07", "question": "How many penitents were involved, and who were they?", "turns_on": "The reports count different groups and distinguish the pardoned penitents from the deferred three.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q07/p1", "position": "Seven penitents were involved, four identified as Jadd ibn Qays, Abū Lubāba, Ḥarām, and Aws.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda give seven; Qatāda's four had promised striving, spending, and charity. {"id": "9:103/q08", "question": "Whom does 'their' refer to, and how general is the command?", "turns_on": "Whether the historical occasion limits the pronoun or the wording yields a general collection rule.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q08/p1", "position": "It first refers to the penitents who confessed, but the command or ruling extends to Muslims who owe charity.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī identifies those confessing sin. {"id": "9:103/q09", "question": "What does 'wealth' mean here?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish ordinary inclusive ownership from narrower regional or technical usages.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q09/p1", "position": "It includes owned property generally, in multiple kinds.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives māl's derivation from acquisition and increase and contrasts singular uniform wealth with plural varied assets. Abū ʿUmar appeals to ordinary Arabic and a Prophetic saying; Abū Qatāda called a garden acquired for armor his first wealth. Some of Daws called clothing and goods al-amwāl, as Abū Hurayra's Khaybar report illustrates."}, {"id": "9:103/q09/p2", "position": "It denotes coined gold and silver.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this usage from others."}, {"id": "9:103/q09/p3", "position": "It means camels specifically.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites the saying that wealth is camels."}, {"id": "9:103/q09/p4", "position": "It denotes livestock generally.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this usage."}, {"id": "9:103/q09/p5", "position": "Gold or silver below the zakat threshold is not called wealth.", "reasons": "Thaʿlab cites a poem about never attaining the threshold."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q10", "question": "What kinds of property may the command cover?", "turns_on": "Whether wealth is taken in its broad owned-property sense or specified by zakat law and intention.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q10/p1", "position": "The plural covers multiple categories, subject to legal specification.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima explains 'from' by zakat being due only on some kinds. {"id": "9:103/q12", "question": "What are the monetary zakat thresholds and rates?", "turns_on": "The disputed increments above silver nisab and the competing gold nisabs.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q12/p1", "position": "Silver reaches nisab at 200 dirhams after a year, with one fortieth due; every excess amount is taxed.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī records agreement that an uqiyya is forty dirhams and five dirhams are due at 200. {"id": "9:103/q13", "question": "What livestock zakat schedules are cited?", "turns_on": "The schedules differ at 121 camels, 301 sheep, and below thirty cattle.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q13/p1", "position": "At five camels one sheep is due; at 121 camels the collector may choose three bint labūn or two ḥiqqas.", "reasons": "Mālik's 121-camel option is shared by ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Salama, Ibn Abī Ḥāzim, and Ibn Dīnār. Al-Qurṭubī reports consensus below five and cites Abū Bakr's letter to Anas for schedules."}, {"id": "9:103/q13/p2", "position": "At 121 camels three bint labūn are due until 130, then one ḥiqqa and two bint labūn.", "reasons": "Ibn Shihāb gives this schedule; Ibn al-Qāsim prefers it."}, {"id": "9:103/q13/p3", "position": "For sheep, three are due at 201 through 399, four at 400, then another per hundred.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites the majority, with agreement on the subsequent hundred increment."}, {"id": "9:103/q13/p4", "position": "For sheep, four are due at 301, five at 401, then another per hundred.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Ḥayy and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī are reported to hold this."}, {"id": "9:103/q13/p5", "position": "For cattle, one yearling is due at thirty and one mature cow at forty.", "reasons": "Muʿādh's Yemen report includes this schedule and a dinar or Maʿāfir cloth from each adult as poll tax; al-Tirmidhī authenticates it. {"id": "9:103/q14", "question": "How are trade goods and hidden assets collected?", "turns_on": "Whether property is visible to collectors, and how initial ownership and public shares are conceived.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q14/p1", "position": "Visible livestock, crops, fruits, and circulating trade goods are collected by officials at their locations.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports the Prophet's collectors visited livestock at watering places; the Thaqīf condition meant no assembly of herds. ʿUmar extended collection to open trade goods and no Companion objected; ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz followed this. For Muslims, a year, nisab, and ownership are required; ʿUmar's rates were quarter-tithe for Muslims, half-tithe for dhimmīs, full tithe for enemies. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz reports half a dinar per twenty from Muslim traders and one from dhimmīs."}, {"id": "9:103/q14/p2", "position": "Owners presented hidden-asset zakat voluntarily; later direct payment to the poor was allowed.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the Prophet and first caliphs received it, because homes and shops could not be searched. ʿUthmān ordered debts paid first and allowed owners to choose recipients."}, {"id": "9:103/q14/p3", "position": "Zakat and similar shares arise when new wealth appears, while the remainder belongs to the worker or owner.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues from 2:29 and 4:5 that wealth might initially be society's, with an individual's share assigned; after ownership settles, further charges are usurpation except emergency needs."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q15", "question": "How did Ibn Zayd identify the people addressed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q15/p1", "position": "They were hypocrites who missed Tabūk, confessed hypocrisy and doubt, and renewed repentance by offering charity.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd links the passage to 9:84's prohibition on prayer over dead hypocrites; a separate report says they had promised to fight and give charity."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q16", "question": "What kind of charity is meant?", "turns_on": "Whether the occasion fixes the kind of alms or the general wording and purifying function indicate prescribed zakat.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q16/p1", "position": "It is the obligatory zakat.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima, al-Jubbāʾī, and many jurists hold this. Al-Ālūsī reports al-Jubbāʾī's concern that rejecting their payment would liken them to hypocrites. Elmalılı allows extra gifts. Asad says state acceptance recognizes Muslim standing."}, {"id": "9:103/q16/p2", "position": "It is a voluntary expiatory gift from the repentant men.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd, Ibn Kaysān, al-Ḥasan and others place it after accepted repentance; al-Rāzī's advocates say a new zakat ruling would break the surrounding passage's coherence. {"id": "9:103/q17", "question": "When and how did fixed zakat become obligatory?", "turns_on": "Whether 9:103 begins zakat's obligation or applies a prior institution.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q17/p1", "position": "This passage establishes a new command to collect obligatory zakat.", "reasons": "Most jurists in al-Rāzī, al-Bursevī, and Kur'an Yolu infer a general ruling."}, {"id": "9:103/q17/p2", "position": "Fixed-threshold zakat was probably obligated in year two after Ramadan, with regular state collection perhaps beginning in year nine.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu distinguishes eight Meccan uses of zakat as a flexible duty from twenty-two definite Medinan uses and twelve of ṣadaqa; it acknowledges uncertainty in the dating. {"id": "9:103/q18", "question": "What social purpose and distribution policy does zakat serve?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q18/p1", "position": "It supplies society's needs while improving individuals and reducing class differences.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares zakat and khums to earlier communal provisions, describes zakat's eight and khums's six recipient classes, and argues public shares should aid people rather than prestige works. {"id": "9:103/q20", "question": "What does purifying them through charity mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the object of cleansing is sin, conduct, property, or inward attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q20/p1", "position": "The charity removes sins, including the stain of staying behind and attachment to wealth.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and many successors identify cleansing of sin; al-Bayḍāwī adds attachment to property as the source of recurrence. Abū ʿAlī compares removing people's moral refuse to cleansing and distinguishes legal impurity from bodily dirt, citing 9:28. Al-Qurṭubī's lexicon defines ṭahūr as pure and purifying. The Study Quran cites prophetic purification with teaching in 2:129, 2:151, 3:164 and 62:2."}, {"id": "9:103/q20/p2", "position": "Purification is obedience and sincerity.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it thus in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim; the action exhibits repentance."}, {"id": "9:103/q20/p3", "position": "In an inward reading it removes attachment to created things and egoic darkness.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī reports purification from the stain of created things; Ruwaym describes cleansing inner secrets and refining souls. {"id": "9:103/q21", "question": "How are the two purification verbs parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the feminine tāʾ refers to ṣadaqa or addresses the Prophet, and whether the verbs are raised or jussive.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q21/p1", "position": "Both verbs address the Prophet, who purifies and develops them by taking charity.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, Abū Isḥāq, Abū ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ālūsī, and later commentators prefer connected second-person address; both can be circumstantial, adjectival with omitted 'by it', or resumed. The presence of bihā strongly favors address in al-Zamakhsharī's argument. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Nasafī say the second verb must be address. Al-Samīn lists syntactic combinations."}, {"id": "9:103/q21/p2", "position": "The first verb describes charity; the second addresses the Prophet or starts a new clause.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers the adjective for the first because the canonical readers raise it, and a new clause for the raised second. Basran grammarians and al-Akhfash allow repetition for emphasis; others make the second circumstantial. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Samīn object to Makkī's mixed parse under coordination, and Abū Ḥayyān says it needs a rare implied subject."}, {"id": "9:103/q21/p3", "position": "The verbs can be jussive as the result of the imperative.", "reasons": "Kufan grammarians favor jussive for a Prophet-addressed verb lacking a pronoun returning to charity; al-Zajjāj gives 'if you take, you purify' and al-Naḥḥās quotes a poetic parallel. Others note the actual raised reading is circumstantial or adjectival."}, {"id": "9:103/q21/p4", "position": "Both verbs can describe charity itself, with bihā emphasizing the charitable cause.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, Basran grammarians, al-Naḥḥās, and al-Qurṭubī allow feminine charity as subject; al-Ṭabrisī and al-Nasafī constrain the second verb to direct address."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q22", "question": "What variant forms of the purification verbs are reported?", "turns_on": "The transmitted case and verbal form, including causative and jussive variants.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q22/p1", "position": "Al-Ḥasan reads a lighter causative form IV of the first verb.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī derive it from aṭhara; some describe a silent ṭāʾ or light initial form."}, {"id": "9:103/q22/p2", "position": "Both verbs, or the first, are read in the jussive as the command's result.", "reasons": "Muslima ibn Muḥārib and Ibn Muḥārib are named for both; al-Kashshāf and later sources report the jussive. {"id": "9:103/q23", "question": "What does 'you sanctify or grow them by it' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether growth refers to status, virtue, wealth, or inward development.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q23/p1", "position": "It elevates them from the rank of hypocrites to sincere believers and increases good deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī and others give the rank change; al-Ālūsī warns that it implies actual hypocrisy, contrary to his sounder view. {"id": "9:103/q25", "question": "What did the Prophet actually say or do when praying for donors?", "turns_on": "Reports distinguish habitual donor prayer, a suggested collection formula, and the specific penitents.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q25/p1", "position": "He prayed for contributors, including the family of Abū Awfā, and sometimes said 'O God, bless them'.", "reasons": "The Abū Awfā reports occur across Ibn Qutayba, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Durr, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī; al-Ṭabrisī notes Bukhārī and Muslim, while al-Qurṭubī cites Muslim.
